document.abstract: This paper presents a nonconventional approach and method for converting naturalistic (non–computer-generated) two-dimensional (2D) video and film material to Stereoscopic 3D. Experimental evidence is presented to show the efficacy of color-based surrogate depth maps for automatic 2D-to-3D conversion aimed at small-screen applications. A semiautomatic 2D-to-3D conversion system (CRC-DMEG), also based on surrogate depth maps, for the conversion of video and film content for commercial projection on large cinema screens is then presented. A major advantage of CRC-DMEG is that it exploits the correlation between the 2D color images and the surrogate depth maps to allow for direct manipulation of the depth of objects in a scene. Another major advantage is that it allows for instant realization of depth details, such as raindrops, foliage, and textures found in carpets. This approach and method minimizes the labor-intensive work associated with the conventional method of rotoscoping. Moreover, the manual task of filling in disoccluded regions is also significantly reduced.

authors.bio: Carlos Vázquez, research scientist, received a B. Eng. and M.Sc. degrees from the Higher Polytechnic Institute José Antonio Echeverría (ISPJAE) in Havana, Cuba, where he also worked as a lecturer and assistant professor. He received a Ph.D. degree in telecommunications from the INRS-EMT, Montréal, Canada, in 2003, following his position as a Research Associate at Concordia University, Montréal, Canada, until 2005. In August 2005 he joined the Communications Research Centre (CRC), which is the Canadian government's primary laboratory for R&D in advanced telecommunications. His research interests are in the areas of 3DTV; stereo and multiview vision systems; image/video representation, sampling and interpolation; image and video coding; and motion/disparity/depth estimation and compensation.
authors.name: Carlos Vazquez

authors.bio: Wa James Tam is a senior research scientist at the CRC. Tam holds a Ph.D. in experimental psychology from York University, Toronto, and has been with the CRC for more than 20 years. Tam's research interest is in human visual perception and its application to the design and development of advanced video systems. One of the first projects that he worked on was eye movements and television viewing. In the early 90s, he co-founded the 3D research program at CRC. He is currently a project leader on 3DTV in the Advanced Video Systems Group in the Broadcast Technologies Branch.
authors.name: Wa James Tam
